prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade exposure reshape labour demand, wages and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: I keep B006 as my preferred single part, judged on the common criteria. It has a clear conceptual contribution: the task-based view of work and the supply-and-demand account of the skill premium. It also has well-identified evidence on how local labour markets adjust to import competition. That combination of framework and credible design is what the 2021 prize rewarded in other settings. The trade-shock evidence has been replicated across countries and has been debated for over a decade. The skill-premium work is about three decades old and the task model over twenty years old, so maturity is not a concern. The questions are central: who bears the cost of technological and trade change, and how persistent those costs are. They also sit squarely within the empirical-policy tradition I know best, which is why I try to hold this ballot to the same standard as the others. Unlike several alternatives, the credited names map onto identifiable strands: Autor for tasks and the China shock, Hanson for the trade-shock design, Katz for the long-run skill-premium framework.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. A three-person cap leaves out Dorn, a central co-author of the trade-shock papers, and also leaves out contributors to the task framework who are not on the credited list. The ballot also combines two strands, technology and trade, so a citation risks being a composite rather than one discovery. Katz's best-known work is entangled with Goldin's, whose 2023 prize covered adjacent ground. The magnitude and persistence of the China shock, and the inference problems with shift-share designs, are still debated.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B006 first but stresses that Autor, Hanson and Dorn jointly carry the China-shock work, that Katz anchors the earlier skill-premium line, and that Levy and Murnane co-developed the task approach but are not credited. He regards a three-person set as defensible but incomplete.
responses.response: I agree this is the real weakness, and I do not think the committee should hide it. Where I differ slightly is on remedy. Swapping Dorn for Katz would narrow the citation to the trade-shock design and make it cleaner as one discovery. But it would drop the long-run skill-premium framework, which supplies the interpretive structure that makes the trade-shock evidence about labour demand and not only about local adjustment. I prefer Autor, Hanson and Katz because the three strands are then each represented by the person most identified with them. I would accept the Dorn variant if colleagues judge that a single-discovery citation matters more than breadth. Levy and Murnane are a genuine omission that the cap forces. The citation should therefore be worded around the evidence and the framework, not as a claim to have credited the whole task lineage.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B006 first and notes that the three-name limit is a real constraint, with a possible Dorn-versus-Katz choice. She adds that Acemoglu's overlapping task-model contribution is already recognised, and that the Goldin and Acemoglu prizes overlap with this ballot.
responses.response: I share the Dorn-versus-Katz question, as above. I would qualify the overlap point, though. The 2024 prize was for work on institutions and prosperity, and the 2023 prize was for the history and drivers of women's labour-market outcomes. Neither prize cited the task-based framework or the import-competition evidence as such. Thematic adjacency should affect timing, but it should not count as prior recognition of this discovery. I do accept that Goldin–Katz complicates Katz's separate credit. That is a reason to describe his contribution precisely, as the skill-premium and education-technology framework, and not to treat it as a general inequality contribution.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B034 first. She argues that BLP demand estimation and dynamic-oligopoly methods are transparent, reproducible, three decades old and used in merger review and antitrust. She credits Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes clearly, while noting sensitivity to numerical implementation and instruments.
responses.response: I agree B034 has cleaner attribution on the BLP core than B006 has, and I ranked it second myself for that reason, so it is my first alternative. Its maturity and practical reach are not in doubt. Where I come out differently is on breadth of scientific consequence. B034 is a methodological toolkit for a particular class of questions, while B006 combines a framework with credible designs on a question that has changed how a whole field and policy debate understand adjustment to technology and trade. The BLP sensitivity to implementation and instruments does not count heavily against it, because it is well documented. But the question of how to treat the dynamic-game strand and Bresnahan's contributions would need settling in the citation. I would not treat the cleaner attribution as outweighing the difference in scientific consequence, but I would take B034 seriously if B006 stalls on credit division.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B032 (Kiyotaki and Moore) first. He argues that collateral-constraint amplification is foundational, was borne out by the 2007–09 crisis, and is distinct from the financial-accelerator work recognised in the 2022 prize. He also flags that his own field affinity should not count as merit.
responses.response: I appreciate the explicit separation of the Kiyotaki–Moore mechanism from the Bernanke–Gertler–Gilchrist line. It is the right way to handle the overlap, and I ranked B032 sixth for the same reason. My reservation is on the empirical side. As I noted in my opening, direct tests of the original model are limited and much of the support is indirect, supplied largely by the post-2008 experience. For a prize I would want the mechanism to be disciplined by evidence to a degree that B006 clearly is and B032 is less clearly. The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises narrows the room for it. If the committee wants a macro-finance part, I would want to see the evidence linking the mechanism to measured outcomes before ranking it above the labour-demand work.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers the Autor–Hanson–Katz breadth citation or a narrower Autor–Dorn–Hanson trade-shock citation, and how to word credit for the task-framework contributors outside the credited list.
How persistent and large the China-shock effects are, and how far shift-share identification concerns qualify the headline estimates.
How the committee weighs recent prizes on adjacent labour, technology and institutions topics, which bear on timing but should not affect merit.
Whether a two-part configuration (for example adding a BLP part) would be better than a single part, given that the cap of three people forces unattractive splits.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship, institutional or collaborator tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is apparent from my supplied profile. I disclose field proximity: I am an empirical labour economist working with Swedish register data and quasi-experimental designs, and my class-size work is cited in the 2021 Scientific Background. This is a methodological affinity that could bias my view of B006. I have tried to apply the same criteria as for other fields, and I do not adjudicate the matter.
